author: Unreal Engine
description:
The Technical Developer Relations team at Epic, based on their experience supporting customers and their own work with Unreal Engine, has identified a selection of cross-discipline indicators that often influence the outcomes of real-time projects. 

Jam-packed with resources, this session recorded at Unreal Fest Chicago 2026 explains what these key indicators are, why they’re important, what types of projects they affect most, where in the lifespan of a project they’re most impactful, and how to implement Epic-recommended best practices. 

Topics covered include optimization, fidelity, scalability, engine version integration, build health, iteration workflows, project settings, and avenues for additional learning. Although each of these topics touches on a number of features that could (or already have) separate deep dives, we spend our time fitting all these pieces together from an implementation-focused perspective.

title: Project Health in Unreal Engine: The Technical Indicators That Matter | Unreal Fest Chicago 2026

author: Unreal Engine
description:
Join us as Christopher Main walks through his workflow for creating an "Online Puzzle Extraction Game" in 7 days as a solo developed project. Utilizing many Unreal Engine systems for extremely fast blueprint multiplayer iteration. This session shows quick tips for concept, retro aesthetics, 3D modeling, rigging, animation, textures, audio and more.

Check out the game yourself here: https://themainstark.itch.io/spinlock
title: How a Solo Dev Made a Blueprint Online Multiplayer Game with UE in 7 Days | Inside Unreal

author: Unreal Engine
description:
By default, Unreal Engine projects fully recook on every invocation: each package to ship is loaded and saved, with partial but not full caching. On large projects, it can take hours for every execution. 

Since UE3, Unreal Engine has supported opt-in iterative cooking, in which only changed packages are loaded and resaved. The legacy version of iterative cooking does not detect all dependencies, however, so some packages are skipped when they should not be and stale data is used at runtime. 

In UE5, we’ve added more robust dependencies into the iterative cook; this new version is now the default in 5.7 and is called incremental cooking to distinguish it from the simpler legacy iterative mode. Incremental cooking has some dependencies (ZenServer, TObjectPtr, programmer guidelines for C++ changes) that are required either for it to be enabled or for it to work correctly. 

In this talk recorded at Unreal Fest Chicago 2026, we present what is necessary to make incremental cook fully en
title: Incremental Cooking in UE 5.7: A Dive Into the UE Cook Pipeline | Unreal Fest Chicago 2026
